segments.say: Ines is standing at the kitchen sink with her sleeves pushed up, washing the last of the dishes, and the radio on the windowsill is playing something she half knows. A choir, singing softly. Then, a line from the end of the song, the whole thing lifts a step higher, and a shiver runs from the back of her neck down along both arms. The hairs on her forearms stand up. She stops, with a wet plate in her hands, and just listens.

A quick word about Ines. She's imagined. She's someone we've pictured together, to keep us company through tonight's ideas. She's thirty-nine, she inspects bridges for a living, and she's the kind of person who notices how things are held together. Nothing about her is meant to stand for any real person, and nothing in her evening is a case study. She's simply here so that the ideas have somewhere to land.

The odd thing is that Ines isn't cold. The kitchen is warm. She isn't frightened, and nothing sad has happened today. And yet her body has just reacted as though something dramatic had occurred, over a few seconds of sound. It's happened to her before, at weddings, in cars, once in a supermarket, and she's never quite known what to make of it.

When she mentions it to her friend Tobias, he laughs and says it never happens to him. He likes music, he says, he just doesn't get that feeling. And that makes Ines wonder. If it's the same song, and the same ears, and the same air, why does one person shiver and another simply enjoy it?

That's the puzzle for tonight. A few seconds of sound, nothing you can touch or eat, nothing that can hurt you, and the body answers as though something important had happened. Hairs lifting, skin tingling, a catch in the throat, sometimes tears.

show.text: A few seconds of sound, and the body answers as if something important had happened.

segments.say: So here's the question Ines is asking, and maybe you've asked it too. Why does a piece of music sometimes send a shiver down your spine? What is the brain doing in those few seconds, and why do some people feel it strongly while others never seem to?

show.sub: Why does music give us chills?

segments.say: Let's be clear from the start. Nothing is wrong with Ines, and nothing is wrong with Tobias. Getting chills from music is a well-studied human experience, and not getting them is too. Neither one says anything about how deeply a person loves music. What the research offers is a way of understanding the experience, not a way of ranking people.

show.sub: This is a normal body doing a normal thing

segments.say: Tonight, we'll explore what scientists mean by chills, and how they measure something so fleeting. We'll look at early experiments with a drug that blocks the body's natural opioids, at brain scans taken while people listened to their favorite pieces, and at the role of anticipation and surprise. We'll hear about who tends to get chills, what the chemistry might be, how poems and films do it too, and why music and memory are so tangled together. And near the end, why singing together matters, and why sad songs can feel so good.

show.title: Tonight, we'll explore
items: Why a pattern can please us
Who gets chills and who doesn't

segments.say: This is a long, calm video, made to keep you company in the evening or as you drift toward sleep. First, we'll spend some time with the science, one idea at a time, with the names and years so you can look things up yourself. Then, near the end, the pace slows right down for a long, gentle wind-down. If you fall asleep along the way, that's perfectly fine. It's what the second half is for.
So let's begin with the shiver itself, and with the simple question of what it is.

Researchers have several names for the experience. Some call it frisson, a French word for a shiver. Some say musical chills, or thrills, or in everyday speech, goosebumps. In the scientific papers, the word you'll most often see is chills, and they define it loosely as a pleasant tingling sensation, often on the back of the neck or the arms, that comes in waves and lasts a few seconds.

The goosebumps are the visible part. At the base of each body hair there's a tiny muscle, and when it contracts, it pulls the hair upright and makes the skin around it bump. In animals with thick fur, the same reflex puffs up the coat to trap warmth or to look bigger. In people, with so little fur left, the reflex is mostly a leftover. It still fires, though, and it fires for more reasons than cold.

show.cap: The skin has a part in it
show.sub: Tiny muscles at the base of each hair

segments.say: In 2011, two Austrian psychologists, Mathias Benedek and Christian Kaernbach, found a way to measure goosebumps objectively. They pointed a small camera at the skin of listeners' forearms and tracked tiny changes in the surface of the skin. People listened to music and watched emotional clips, and the goosebumps they recorded lined up with moments when listeners said they felt moved, and not just with moments when they felt chilly.

show.what: Measured goosebumps with a small camera and found they went with moments of being moved

segments.say: Chills are rarely just a skin event. Researchers who attach sensors to listeners during strong musical moments often see a short burst of arousal. The heart rate shifts. Breathing changes. The skin's electrical conductance, a sign of tiny changes in sweat, jumps. In other words, the body shows the same sort of excitement it might show in a thrilling moment, even though the listener is sitting perfectly still.

That's worth noticing. Arousal usually has a bad reputation, as though it always meant stress. But arousal is simply the body getting ready. In a frightening moment it points toward fear, and in a musical moment it points toward delight. The same physical system can carry either message, and the music seems to steer it toward the second.

Think of Ines at the sink again. The warm lamp. The quiet room. A tune she half knows. Nothing around her has changed, and yet her body has told her, in a few seconds, that something mattered. That mismatch between the quiet scene and the strong reaction is exactly what has made the subject so interesting to researchers.

How common are chills? It depends on how the question is asked, which is a good habit to keep in mind with any statistic. In surveys, a majority of people say they've felt them, and some reports put the share well above half. But not everyone does, and the people who don't are not missing anything about hearing. We'll meet some of those listeners later tonight.

Many people who do get chills describe going back to the same piece again and again, to feel it. They know exactly which moment it will arrive. Some can point to the very bar. And for a long time, that was simply something people said about themselves. In the second half of the twentieth century, researchers began to ask whether it could be studied.

How do you study a feeling that lasts four seconds and can't be forced? Early researchers used a simple trick. They asked people to bring their own favorite music, the pieces that reliably gave them chills, and then they recorded what happened in the body and the brain while those pieces played. Starting from a person's own favorite turns out to work far better than choosing the music for them.

It matters because taste is personal. A piece that sends a wave through one listener leaves another untouched, and a researcher who plays the same recording to everyone will mostly measure the average of many different tastes. By letting people choose, scientists could look at what the brain does when the pleasure is real, rather than what it does when music is merely played.

Ines, meanwhile, dries her hands and turns the radio up a little. She wants to hear that passage again, to see whether it will do it a second time. It does, almost. A smaller shiver. And she doesn't know it yet, but she has just run a very small version of an experiment that scientists have been running, with far more equipment, for more than forty years.
That's where we'll go next, to a small and cleverly simple experiment from 1980, one that asked whether the shiver had anything to do with the body's own natural painkillers.
